Artificial Intelligence.explanation: AI teaches computers to think, learn, and make decisions like humans
points: Encompasses symbolic rules, statistical learning, neural networks and hybrid approaches
Powers recommendation engines, autonomous driving, medical image analysis, fraud detection and chat interfaces
Most current systems remain narrow / task-specific rather than generally intelligent
Long-term research targets safe AGI while near-term focus lies on reliability and misuse prevention
Progress heavily tied to exponential growth in compute, data volume and algorithmic efficiency

Machine Learning.explanation: ML lets computers learn from data without being explicitly programmed for every task
points: Learns generalizable patterns from examples instead of hand-written if-then rules
Main families: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, self-supervised, semi-supervised
Drives search ranking, ad targeting, churn prediction, demand forecasting, anomaly detection
Model quality is extremely sensitive to training data distribution, label accuracy and coverage
Requires deliberate validation (time-split, stratified CV, OOD testing) to estimate deployment performance

Neural Networks.explanation: Neural networks are inspired by the brain and learn to recognize patterns in data
points: Layers of weighted connections + non-linear activations allow complex function approximation
Theoretical universal approximation property holds given enough neurons and layers
Backbone architecture for nearly all leading vision, language and audio models since ~2012
Training frontier-scale models routinely consumes thousands of GPU/TPU-days
Black-box optimization behavior motivates large interpretability and reverse-engineering efforts

Deep Learning.explanation: Deep learning stacks many neural network layers to solve complex AI problems
points: Discovers hierarchical representations automatically from raw pixels, waveforms or tokens
Delivered super-human performance on ImageNet, speech recognition, Go, protein structure prediction
Scaling laws relate performance gains to model size, dataset size and compute budget
Overfitting combated via dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, mixup, CutMix, stochastic depth
Very deep architectures rely on residual connections, normalization layers and careful initialization

Computer Vision.explanation: Computer vision lets machines see and understand images and video like humans do
points: Core problems: classification, detection, segmentation, pose estimation, optical flow, tracking, depth
Modern pipelines dominated by CNNs → Vision Transformers → hybrid Conv-Transformer designs
Deployed at scale in self-driving cars, radiology, facial recognition, inventory robots, AR/VR
Brittle under domain shift, adversarial patches, extreme lighting, heavy occlusion, rare classes
Strong trend toward foundation models pretrained on massive image–text or video–text pairs

NLP.explanation: Natural Language Processing helps computers read, understand, and generate human language
points: Spans tokenization, POS tagging, NER, sentiment, translation, summarization, QA, dialogue, reasoning
Transformer-based large autoregressive / masked language models dominate since 2018
Enables virtual assistants, real-time translation, content moderation, legal search, code completion
Low-resource languages, dialects, code-mixing, sarcasm, long-document understanding remain hard
Highly vulnerable to prompt injection, jailbreaks, sycophancy, hallucination, bias leakage

Reinforcement Learning.explanation: RL trains AI by rewarding good decisions like teaching a dog new tricks with treats
points: Learns policies or value functions through environment interaction and delayed rewards
Landmark results: AlphaGo/AlphaZero, Dota 2, StarCraft, dexterous robot manipulation, chip floorplanning
Sample inefficiency often requires millions to billions of environment steps to learn
Exploration addressed via epsilon-greedy, entropy regularization, curiosity, count-based bonuses
Deep RL still suffers from brittle training, reward hacking and high variance in policy gradients

Generative AI.explanation: Generative AI creates new content: text, images, audio, code, and video from scratch
points: Major families: autoregressive transformers, diffusion models, GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows
Produced photorealistic images (Midjourney, Flux), coherent long text (Claude, GPT-4o), music & video
Text-to-X conditioning allows style, composition and subject control via natural language
Training extremely compute hungry; inference often accelerated via quantization, distillation, speculation
Intense debate around training data copyright, deepfake detection, provenance watermarking

Transfer Learning.explanation: Transfer learning reuses knowledge from one AI task to speed up solving another
points: Pre-train once on broad data → fine-tune on target task with far less labeled data
Standard recipe that enabled modern CV (ImageNet → downstream) and NLP (BERT/GPT → fine-tune)
Reduces annotation cost and training time by 10–100× in many domains
Negative transfer occurs when source and target distributions are too dissimilar
Parameter-efficient variants (LoRA, DoRA, adapters, prompt/prefix tuning) dominate for ≥70B models

AI Agents.explanation: AI agents can reason, plan, and take actions autonomously to complete complex tasks
points: Usually LLM backbone + memory + tools (search, code, calculator) + planning/reflection loop
Prototypes: Auto-GPT, LangGraph, OpenAI o1 reasoning mode, robotics task decomposition
Aims at long-horizon autonomy instead of single-turn Q&A or classification
Frequent issues: looping, hallucinated actions, context overflow, poor error recovery
Safety concerns escalate dramatically with tool access and real-world actuators

Supervised Learning.explanation: Supervised learning trains AI using labeled examples with known correct answers
points: Most production ML today is supervised classification or regression
Bottleneck usually high-quality labeled data — annotation cost and label noise common
Training almost always uses mini-batch stochastic gradient descent variants
Real datasets frequently show severe imbalance, long-tail distribution, noisy/incorrect labels
Mitigations include re-weighting, focal loss, data augmentation, label smoothing, distillation

Unsupervised Learning.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in data without any labeled examples
points: Families: clustering, density estimation, dimensionality reduction, representation learning
Applications: customer segmentation, outlier detection, feature discovery, pre-training
Intrinsic evaluation metrics (silhouette, reconstruction error, log-likelihood) often noisy
Frequently serves as warm-start or auxiliary task before supervised fine-tuning
Scaling to trillion-token unlabeled corpora remains an important research direction

Self-supervised Learning.explanation: Self-supervised learning creates its own labels from raw data to train on
points: Popular pretext tasks: masked prediction, contrastive learning, rotation, jigsaw, denoising
Produced many strong vision (DINOv2, MAE) and multimodal (data2vec, CLIP) backbones
Learns transferable representations from internet-scale unlabeled image/text/audio/video
Scaling laws show predictable gains from model size, data volume and pretext design
Augmentation strategy, negative sampling and loss formulation still critically important

Few-shot Learning.explanation: Few-shot learning teaches AI to recognize new concepts from just a handful of examples
points: Strategies: meta-learning (MAML), metric learning (Prototypical Nets), prompt conditioning
Essential in domains with very sparse labels: rare diseases, emerging products, new attack types
Large language models perform few-shot classification via in-context examples
Human-level few-shot generalization on arbitrary new concepts remains far away
Synthetic data, better pre-training and retrieval augmentation improve few-shot results

Zero-shot Learning.explanation: Zero-shot learning allows AI to handle tasks it was never explicitly trained on
points: Relies on side information: semantic embeddings, attributes, class descriptions in natural language
Contrastive image–text models (CLIP, ALIGN) enabled strong zero-shot image classification
LLMs solve zero-shot QA, classification, translation via well-crafted prompts
Performance collapses when target domain or task lies outside pre-training coverage
Prompt brittleness, ambiguous instructions and distributional shift are primary failure modes

Explainable AI.explanation: XAI makes AI decisions transparent and understandable to humans
points: Methods include LIME, SHAP, integrated gradients, attention rollout, counterfactuals
Mandatory or strongly desired in healthcare, finance, justice, safety-critical automation
Common tension: more interpretable models (trees, rules) usually less accurate
Post-hoc explanations can be unstable, misleading or gamed with small input perturbations
Mechanistic interpretability aims for faithful reverse-engineering of network computations

AI Safety.explanation: AI safety research ensures powerful AI systems remain aligned with human values and goals
points: Near-term: bias mitigation, jailbreak resistance, reliability, adversarial robustness
Long-term: avoiding goal misgeneralization, scalable oversight, corrigibility, value learning
Evaluation techniques: red-teaming, debate protocols, weak-to-strong generalization probes
Mechanistic interpretability and activation engineering are key scientific tools
Compute governance, international coordination and whistleblower protections gaining traction

AI Alignment.explanation: Alignment ensures that what AI optimizes for matches what humans actually want
points: Classic problems: specification gaming, proxy reward exploitation, inner misalignment
Dominant current method: RLHF → reward modeling → PPO optimization
Alternatives under exploration: constitutional AI, debate, recursive reward modeling, RLAIF
Scalable oversight becomes necessary once models exceed median human capability
Core open challenge: defining, preserving and loading coherent human values at superintelligence scale

AI Ethics.explanation: AI ethics studies the moral implications of building and deploying AI systems
points: Key themes: fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, autonomy, responsibility
Addresses differential impact on marginalized groups, surveillance capitalism, labor displacement
Frameworks: value-sensitive design, ethics-by-design, stakeholder consultation, impact assessment
Tension between open research, commercial incentives and dual-use technology risks
Increasing calls for binding regulation, independent auditing and public deliberation

Bias in AI.explanation: AI bias happens when training data contains unfair patterns that the model learns and repeats
points: Sources: historical discrimination, selection bias, label bias, proxy features, measurement error
Manifests in hiring tools, credit scoring, facial analysis, recidivism prediction, ad targeting
Fairness definitions conflict (demographic parity vs equal opportunity vs equalized odds…)
Mitigation toolbox: re-sampling, adversarial debiasing, post-processing, causal intervention
Bias often re-emerges after deployment when data distributions drift or populations change

Adversarial Examples.explanation: Adversarial examples are inputs carefully crafted to fool AI models into making mistakes
points: Small norm-bounded perturbations cause confident misclassification
Threat vector for vision (stop-sign attacks), audio (speech command spoofing), text (toxic bypass)
Defenses: adversarial training, randomized smoothing, certified robustness, input purification
Adversarial vulnerability appears inherent to high-dimensional linear classifiers
Transferability across models and black-box query attacks remain practical concerns

Gradient Descent.explanation: Gradient descent is the algorithm that iteratively adjusts model weights to minimize error
points: Dominant optimizers: SGD+momentum, Adam, AdamW, Lion, Sophia, Adafactor
Learning rate warm-up, cosine decay, OneCycle policy improve convergence speed & stability
Second-order / quasi-Newton methods (K-FAC, Shampoo) show promise but scale poorly
Generalization often better when converging to flatter minima in the loss landscape
Very large batch sizes require learning rate scaling and sometimes LARS/LAMB optimizers

Attention Mechanism.explanation: Attention lets AI models focus on the most relevant parts of input when producing output
points: Scaled dot-product self-attention enables parallel sequence processing
Multi-head attention learns different semantic subspaces simultaneously
Core innovation that made Transformers outperform RNNs on long sequences
Efficiency variants: sparse, linear, FlashAttention-2, multi-query/grouped-query
Long-context modeling still limited; state-space models and hybrid approaches gaining ground

Convolutional Neural Net.explanation: CNNs use filters to detect visual patterns making them ideal for image recognition tasks
points: Local receptive fields + weight sharing → translation equivariance and parameter efficiency
Evolution: LeNet → AlexNet → VGG → ResNet → EfficientNet → ConvNeXt → modern hybrids
Still competitive with ViTs on smaller datasets or when compute is constrained
Extensions: depthwise-separable, dilated/atrous, deformable, 3D convolutions for video/volumetric data
Hybrid CNN-Transformer backbones frequently win efficiency-accuracy trade-offs

Diffusion Model.explanation: Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a gradual noising process
points: Currently produce highest-fidelity text-to-image results (Stable Diffusion 3, Flux, Imagen 3)
Sampling speed improved via DDIM, latent diffusion, consistency models, flow matching
Classifier-free guidance strongly boosts prompt adherence without auxiliary classifier
Training compute-intensive but parallelizable; inference can be distilled or quantized
Rapidly expanding to video, 3D generation, protein design, time-series, audio synthesis

Transformer.explanation: Transformers process entire sequences in parallel using self-attention instead of recurrence
points: Replaced RNNs as dominant sequence model for language, vision, audio, biology
Variants: encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT), encoder-decoder (T5, BART)
Scaling laws predict performance from parameters, data and compute — very predictable returns
Context window limitations addressed via RoPE, ALiBi, sparse attention, ring attention
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers enable trillion-parameter models with manageable inference cost

Large Language Model.explanation: LLMs are massive transformer models pretrained on internet-scale text corpora
points: Emergent abilities: in-context learning, chain-of-thought, tool use appear at ~50–100B scale
Frontier examples (2025): GPT-4o, Claude 3.5/4, Gemini 2, Grok-2/3, Llama 4, Mistral Large
Instruction-tuning + preference optimization (RLHF/RLAIF/DPO) align helpful & honest behavior
Inference cost/latency/energy still major hurdles for real-time widespread deployment
Open-weight models accelerate research but amplify misuse and distillation risks

Federated Learning.explanation: Federated learning trains AI across many devices without sharing private data centrally
points: Keeps raw user data on-device; only model updates (gradients) leave the device
Deployed in mobile keyboards (Gboard), healthcare cross-hospital models, finance
Challenges: non-IID data, client heterogeneity, communication cost, stragglers
Defenses against poisoning and inference attacks (differential privacy + secure aggregation)
Personalization via hybrid global + local adaptation is common in production

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedba.explanation: RLHF aligns language models using human preference data via reward modeling and policy optimization
points: Three stages: supervised fine-tuning → reward model training → PPO / DPO optimization
Used to align ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama-2-chat, Grok — dramatically improved helpfulness
Alternatives: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization, SPIN
Scaling human feedback is expensive; synthetic preferences and AI feedback (RLAIF) emerging
Reward hacking, sycophancy, jailbreak vulnerability remain difficult to eliminate

Multimodal AI.explanation: Multimodal AI understands and generates multiple types of data like text, images, and audio
points: Examples: GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5/2, Claude 3.5, LLaVA, Kosmos-2, Chameleon, ImageBind
Enables image captioning, visual QA, document understanding, video summarization, speech+vision
Training usually involves contrastive, masked or next-token prediction across modalities
Unified tokenization / discrete autoencoders help bridge different data types
Long-context multimodal understanding still severely limited by memory and compute

Overfitting.explanation: Overfitting is when a model memorizes training data but fails to generalize to new examples
points: Symptoms: large train–validation performance gap, poor OOD / test-set accuracy
Causes: excessive capacity, insufficient regularization, data leakage, low dataset diversity
Mitigated by early stopping, strong regularization, data augmentation, ensemble methods
Double descent phenomenon shows test error can decrease again after overfitting peak
Modern large models often interpolate training data yet still generalize surprisingly well

Regularization.explanation: Regularization adds penalties to prevent AI models from becoming too complex and overfitting
points: Common forms: L1 (Lasso), L2 (weight decay), dropout, stochastic depth, label smoothing
Modern favorite: decoupled weight decay (AdamW) + large learning rate warm-up
Data-based regularization: augmentation (AutoAugment, RandAugment, AugMix)
Architecture-based: batch/layer norm, residual connections, squeeze-excitation
Too much regularization can cause underfitting or optimization instability

Hyperparameter Tuning.explanation: Hyperparameter tuning finds the best settings to maximize an AI model's performance
points: Key hyperparameters: learning rate, batch size, weight decay, dropout rate, architecture depth/width
Popular methods: grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization (Optuna, Hyperopt)
Population-based training (PBT), ASHA, multi-fidelity methods scale better to clusters
Modern deep models often most sensitive to learning rate schedule and optimizer choice
Over-tuning on validation set can indirectly leak test-set information

Backpropagation.explanation: Backpropagation calculates how much each weight contributed to an error and adjusts accordingly
points: Efficiently computes exact gradients via chain rule through the computation graph
Autograd systems (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) automate forward + backward passes
Vanishing/exploding gradients historically limited depth; residuals & normalization largely solved it
Higher-order gradients and meta-gradients enable MAML, hypernetwork training, etc.
Memory-efficient alternatives (gradient checkpointing, activation recomputation) critical at scale

GAN.explanation: Generative Adversarial Networks pit a generator against a discriminator to create realistic content
points: Adversarial training creates a minimax game where generator improves by fooling an increasingly skilled discriminator
Produced early photorealistic faces, art and style transfer (ProGAN, StyleGAN series, BigGAN)
Training instability, mode collapse and evaluation difficulty (no direct likelihood) are classic pain points
Conditional, cycle-consistent, progressive growing and adaptive versions addressed many limitations
Largely overtaken by diffusion models for state-of-the-art unconditional and guided image synthesis in recent years

LSTM.explanation: Long Short-Term Memory networks solve the vanishing gradient problem in long sequences
points: Cell state plus input/forget/output gates allow selective long-range information retention
Dominant sequence model for speech, translation, time-series from ~2014 until Transformers took over
Still appears in embedded systems, real-time signal processing and some legacy production pipelines
Sequential computation prevents full parallelization → slower training/inference than attention-based models
Recent variants (xLSTM, sLSTM, mLSTM) try to bring matrix memory and better parallelization to LSTM-like cells

Random Forest.explanation: Random forests combine many decision trees to make more accurate and stable predictions
points: Ensemble via bagging + random feature selection at splits reduces variance and correlation
Very strong baseline on tabular/structured data with almost no tuning required
Built-in feature importance (permutation or Gini-based) aids interpretability
Robust to outliers, missing values (with surrogate splits) and mixed data types
Inference latency grows with number of trees; usually outperformed by gradient boosting on accuracy

Gradient Boosting.explanation: Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting errors of the previous ones
points: Leading tabular ML algorithms for years: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, HistGradientBoosting
Minimizes differentiable loss via functional gradient descent → extremely flexible
Strong regularization (shrinkage/learning rate, subsampling, max depth) prevents overfitting
Native categorical support (ordered target stats in CatBoost, optimal splitting in LightGBM)
Faster training than deep models on medium-sized tabular data; often wins Kaggle tabular competitions

F1 Score.explanation: The F1 score balances precision and recall into a single model performance metric
points: Harmonic mean → penalizes extreme imbalance between precision and recall more than arithmetic mean
Standard metric for imbalanced classification (fraud, rare event detection, NER, information retrieval)
Macro-F1 treats all classes equally; micro-F1 aggregates counts globally; weighted-F1 most common multi-class variant
Can mask poor performance on minority classes when majority dominates
Matthews correlation coefficient or Cohen’s kappa sometimes preferred for very skewed problems

Confusion Matrix.explanation: A confusion matrix shows how many predictions were correct and which errors were made
points: N×N table (rows = true class, columns = predicted class) reveals per-class error patterns
Direct source for accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, false discovery rate, etc.
Normalized versions (row-wise = recall, column-wise = precision) make comparison easier
Heatmap visualization quickly highlights systematic confusions (e.g. 5↔3 in digit recognition)
Extremely useful for debugging multi-class models before trusting aggregate metrics

ROC Curve & AUC.explanation: The ROC curve shows the tradeoff between true positive rate and false positive rate; AUC summarizes it
points: Threshold-independent view of binary classifier ranking ability
AUC = probability that random positive ranks higher than random negative
Robust to class imbalance (unlike accuracy); AUC ≈ 0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect
Precision-recall curve + AUPRC usually more informative when positives are very rare
Can be misleadingly high when many score ties exist or when operating point is irrelevant

Feature Engineering.explanation: Feature engineering transforms raw data into meaningful inputs that help AI learn better
points: Frequently the highest-leverage step in traditional ML pipelines and tabular competitions
Techniques include binning, polynomial/interaction terms, target encoding, cyclical features, embeddings
Domain-specific features (ratios, differences, time-based aggregates) often beat automatic methods
Feature selection (mutual information, permutation importance, Boruta, recursive elimination) cuts noise
Tree-based models reduce (but rarely eliminate) the need for heavy manual engineering

AutoML.explanation: AutoML automatically selects and tunes the best machine learning pipeline for a task
points: Systems: AutoGluon, H2O AutoML, TPOT, FLAML, Auto-sklearn, Google Cloud AutoML, Vertex AI
Searches algorithms, preprocessors, hyperparameters, stacking/ensembling strategies
Often beats hand-crafted models on tabular data when given reasonable compute budget
Struggles more with vision, NLP, custom preprocessing or very small datasets
Production concerns include pipeline reproducibility, auditability and explanation of chosen model

Edge AI.explanation: Edge AI runs machine learning models directly on devices rather than in the cloud
points: Benefits: ultra-low latency, offline operation, privacy (no data transmission), bandwidth savings
Target hardware: smartphones, IoT sensors, cameras, wearables, industrial controllers, drones
Depends heavily on quantization (INT8/4), pruning, distillation, TensorFlow Lite Micro, ONNX
Hardware accelerators (Apple Neural Engine, Google Edge TPU, Hailo, Qualcomm Hexagon) critical
Core engineering trade-off: accuracy vs model size vs power vs latency

World Model.explanation: World models let AI simulate and predict outcomes in an environment to plan ahead
points: Learns dynamics via video prediction, state transition modeling or reward prediction
Powers DreamerV3 (Atari/Sim), Genie, Sora-like video generation as implicit world models
Planning happens in imagination/latent space → far fewer real environment interactions
Usually trained with reconstruction + consistency or contrastive objectives
Scaling high-fidelity video generation dramatically improves world model quality

Q-Learning.explanation: Q-learning teaches agents the value of taking actions in states to maximize future reward
points: Tabular or approximated action-value function learned off-policy
Deep Q-Network (DQN) breakthrough combined CNNs + experience replay + target network
Improvements: Double DQN, Dueling, Prioritized Replay, Noisy Nets, Rainbow ensemble
Requires large replay memory and careful exploration schedule
Largely replaced by actor-critic methods in continuous/high-dimensional action domains

Policy Gradient.explanation: Policy gradient methods optimize the AI policy directly using gradient ascent
points: REINFORCE baseline: policy gradient theorem + variance reduction via advantage
Actor-critic (A2C/A3C) adds value critic to stabilize training
PPO clips objective for monotonic improvement → became industry standard for stability
TRPO / natural PG use trust-region constraint to avoid destructive steps
Strong in continuous control; combines well with off-policy replay (SAC, TD3)

Principal Component Analysis.explanation: PCA reduces data dimensions while preserving the most important patterns and variance
points: Finds orthogonal axes (principal components) of maximum variance via SVD or eigendecomposition
Classic unsupervised dimensionality reduction for visualization, denoising, compression
Linear method → kernel PCA, autoencoder-based nonlinear extensions exist
Requires centering/standardization; sensitive to outliers and scale
Explained variance ratio guides choice of number of components to keep

Clustering.explanation: Clustering groups similar data points together without using any predefined labels
points: Algorithms: k-means (centroid), DBSCAN/HDBSCAN (density), GMM (probabilistic), spectral
Applications: market segmentation, image compression, anomaly grouping, topic discovery
Number of clusters often chosen via elbow, silhouette, gap statistic or domain knowledge
Density-based methods handle noise and arbitrary shapes better than k-means
Downstream task performance or qualitative inspection most common evaluation

Time Series Forecasting.explanation: AI forecasting models predict future values based on patterns in historical time data
points: Traditional: ARIMA/SARIMA, Prophet; ML: XGBoost with lags, N-BEATS, TFT, PatchTST
Deep models excel at multivariate, long-horizon, probabilistic forecasting
Benchmarks: M4/M5, Monash archive, electricity, traffic, weather, ETT datasets
Seasonality, exogenous variables, missing data, concept drift are frequent issues
Quantile/ distribution heads increasingly standard for uncertainty estimation

Anomaly Detection.explanation: Anomaly detection identifies unusual patterns that deviate from normal expected behavior
points: Methods: isolation forest, autoencoders, one-class SVM, LOF, GAN-based reconstruction
Key domains: fraud, predictive maintenance, network intrusion, manufacturing defects
Mostly unsupervised or semi-supervised (normal data abundant, anomalies rare)
Metrics: precision@K, ROC-AUC-PR, F1@K due to extreme imbalance
Contextual / collective anomalies need specialized sequence or graph methods

Recommendation System.explanation: Recommendation systems predict what a user will like based on their history and behavior
points: Collaborative filtering, content-based, hybrid, knowledge-based approaches
Modern: two-tower models, neural CF, Wide & Deep, DeepFM, session-based transformers
Production: candidate generation → ranking → re-ranking + diversity stages
Cold-start mitigated via side information, exploration, meta-learning
Offline metrics (NDCG, Recall@K) + online A/B tests (CTR, conversion, retention)

Text Classification.explanation: Text classification automatically assigns categories or labels to pieces of text
points: Tasks: sentiment, topic, spam, toxicity, intent, news categorization
Current SOTA: fine-tune DeBERTa-v3, ELECTRA, Longformer or large LLM prompting
Few-shot / zero-shot via large models with structured prompts
Imbalance handled via focal loss, class weighting, oversampling
Multilabel setting uses sigmoid + binary cross-entropy

Named Entity Recognition.explanation: NER identifies and classifies names, dates, places, and organizations in text
points: Datasets: CoNLL-2003, OntoNotes, ACE, Few-NERD, multilingual WikiANN
Transformer + CRF or span-based (GlobalPointer, W2NER) near human performance
Nested entities, emerging names, code-mixed text, long documents still difficult
Zero/few-shot NER via large language models + prompt engineering improving fast
BIO/ES/BILOU tagging schemes; span classification often more robust

Sentiment Analysis.explanation: Sentiment analysis detects whether text is positive, negative, or neutral in tone
points: Levels: document, sentence, aspect-based (e.g. food good, service bad)
Modern: transformer fine-tuning or LLM with chain-of-thought for nuance
Sarcasm, negation, emojis, implicit sentiment, domain shift cause errors
Multilingual performance lags in low-resource languages
Aspect-based and emotion-augmented variants add granularity

Text-to-Speech.explanation: TTS synthesizes natural-sounding speech audio from plain text input
points: Pipeline: text → phoneme/G2P → acoustic → vocoder (HiFi-GAN, WaveGlow)
End-to-end leaders: VITS, NaturalSpeech 2, Mega-TTS, Vall-E X, StyleTTS 2
Zero-shot cloning, prosody/emotion control, multilingual support advancing rapidly
Evaluation: MOS, WER (ASR on output), speaker similarity, real-time latency
Low-latency streaming TTS still challenging for expressive models

Speech Recognition.explanation: Speech recognition converts spoken audio into text as accurately as a human transcriber
points: End-to-end: CTC, RNN-T/Transducer, LAS; Conformer + Whisper-style models
Whisper (multilingual weak supervision) set new bar for robustness and coverage
Accents, noise, overlap, code-switching, domain mismatch remain hard
Self-supervised pre-training (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT) key to low-resource ASR
Streaming real-time systems use RNN-T / Zipformer architectures

Image Segmentation.explanation: Image segmentation labels every pixel in an image with a class it belongs to
points: Semantic, instance, panoptic; U-Net → DeepLab → SegFormer → SAM family
Segment Anything Model (SAM / SAM 2) enables promptable zero-shot segmentation
Medical imaging, autonomous driving, remote sensing are primary applications
Pixel-level annotation expensive → weak supervision, SAM-assisted labeling help
Real-time segmentation critical for robotics and video pipelines

Object Detection.explanation: Object detection identifies and draws bounding boxes around multiple objects in images
points: One-stage (YOLOv8–v10, RT-DETR), two-stage (Faster R-CNN), transformer (DETR, DINO)
Metrics: mAP@0.5:0.95 (COCO), speed (FPS), small/medium/large AP
Open-vocabulary: OWLv2, Grounding DINO detect arbitrary text-described objects
Real-time edge models prioritize YOLO, NanoSAM, RT-DETR variants
Dense prediction heads and query-based decoders dominate recent advances

Knowledge Distillation.explanation: Distillation trains a small student model to mimic the behavior of a large teacher model
points: Loss usually combines hard labels + soft teacher logits (KL divergence)
Variants: offline (fixed teacher), online (joint training), self-distillation
Effective for compressing 70B+ LLMs into 7–13B range with minimal drop
Intermediate layer alignment, attention distillation, data-free variants exist
Distilled models often more robust and calibrate better than small models trained from scratch

Quantization.explanation: Quantization reduces model weight precision from 32-bit to 8-bit or 4-bit for speed and size
points: Post-training quantization (PTQ) vs quantization-aware training (QAT)
Popular formats: INT8, INT4, NF4, FP8; mixed-precision common for sensitive layers
Modern methods (GPTQ, AWQ, SpQR) achieve near-lossless 4-bit inference
Speedups of 2–4× and memory reduction of 4–8× typical on GPU/CPU
Activation quantization and per-token dynamic scaling further improve results

Retrieval-Augmented Generation.explanation: RAG combines retrieval of relevant documents with generation to reduce hallucination
points: Retrieves top-k passages → augments context → generates grounded answer
Greatly improves factual accuracy and allows updating knowledge without retraining
Components: dense retriever (DPR, ColBERT), sparse retriever (BM25), reranker, generator
Challenges: retrieval recall, long-context noise, chunking strategy, staleness
Advanced variants: iterative retrieval, self-RAG, corrective RAG, graph RAG

Mixture of Experts.explanation: MoE sparsely activates only a subset of parameters for each input token
points: Enables trillion-parameter models with active parameter count similar to dense 100B
Routing usually learned top-k softmax over expert scores + load balancing loss
Used in Mixtral 8×22B, DBRX, Grok-1, DeepSeek-V2, future frontier models
Inference cost comparable to dense model of same active size; training more communication heavy
Expert specialization emerges but can lead to routing collapse without careful regularization
